the Kinect depth sensor has stochastic error that is affected by both the location of the pixel being measured and the distance to the object.

the stochastic nature and magnitude of the Kinect error varies with the depth of the measured object, the radial location of the object in the field of view, and the axis of the measurement.

the stochastic characteristics of the Kinect depth sensing device, which is a crucial component of the Kinect's ability to accurately measure depth.
the characterization of Kinect depth sensor error, and the development and presentation of error models for each axis direction.
the stochastic nature of Kinect measurement errors, as well as their effects on the accuracy of Kinect-based measurements.

the stochastic error characteristics of Kinect are affected mostly by the location and distance of the object being measured, though radial factors, as well, must be considered.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have developed an improved statistical model for the Kinect depth error, and we have developed and validated the use of a novel 3-D checkerboard to measure the Kinect error in the horizontal and vertical directions.

the proposed model is more accurate than the existing models for Kinect depth error, especially for large depths, and the proposed model can also be used to estimate the depth error of the Kinect sensor for any given pixel location.
we have presented a more accurate model for the Kinect error, which is based on statistical analysis of the data and is applicable to the entire field of vision.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the stochastic nature and magnitude of the Kinect measurement errors can be accurately modeled and predicted using the presented methodology.
the Kinect error distribution is dependent on both the radial distance and the depth value, and that the error is not constant across the entire field-of-view.
the Kinect error model is not a single function, as has been previously reported, but rather a collection of multiple models, each of which is a function of depth and location.
